public_rationale: Part of this holds. Two days before the post, the WSJ reported OpenAI's internal plan to spend $121 billion on research compute (e1). Earlier coverage did say OpenAI would turn profitable by 2030 (e3). But the WSJ figure is for one year, 2028. It is not spending 'in the next two years': a summary of the same data puts 2026 training costs at about $25 billion (e2). The coverage also did give a reason besides efficiency. Fortune said the turnaround rests on revenue growing to about $200 billion by 2030 (e4). Zitron may think that reason is weak, but it is there. The April WSJ piece itself put break-even in 'the 2030s' (e5). So the figure and the media claim hold, but the time frame and 'no explanation anywhere' do not.
limitations: If 'in the next two years' meant 'two years from now' (2028), the figure part would be fully supported.
The WSJ original was read through a Dow Jones reprint. The year-by-year training figures come from a secondary summary.
How good the explanations are was not graded.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI plans to burn $121 billion on training compute in the next two years, and the media says it will somehow break even in 2030, though there is no explanation anywhere of how beyond vague statements about efficiency.

statement.excerpt: It’s fucking weird that OpenAI plans to burn $121 billion in the next two years on compute for training its models, and that the media’s response is to say that somehow it will break even in 2030, even though there’s no actual explanation anywhere as to how that might happen other than vague statements about “efficiency.”

no actual explanation anywhere as to how
our_interpretation: The $121 billion figure is the one the Wall Street Journal reported on 2026-04-06, two days before the post, from OpenAI's investor documents. I treat 'compute for training' and the WSJ's 'computing power for AI research' as the same thing.
Plain reading of 'in the next two years': spending over the roughly two years after April 2026, not one year further out. Ed Zitron did not say which he meant.
The media part holds if mainstream outlets reported that OpenAI expects to break even or turn profitable around 2030.
The 'no explanation anywhere other than efficiency' part is partly his opinion. I test only whether coverage gave reasons other than efficiency, such as revenue growth, ads or subscriber conversion.
Target period: OpenAI's plans and the coverage as they stood before the post, starting with the November 2025 WSJ-based reporting on 2030 profitability.
criteria.support_condition: Credible reports before the post show that OpenAI planned about $121 billion of research or training compute within the two-year window he named, that the media reported break-even around 2030, and that the coverage gave no reason beyond efficiency.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reports show the $121 billion is for a different period than he described, or that no outlet reported break-even around 2030, or that the coverage explained the path to profit with concrete drivers other than efficiency.
